posts.caption: The braids took forty minutes, the sheen spray took half a can, and the trailer smelled like peppermint by the time we pulled in. She stepped into the ring like she'd been born under a spotlight. Then the judge asked for a canter and she remembered a horse-eating shadow by the far fence. We left the ring at a speed the announcer called 'enthusiastic.' I kept the braids in until Tuesday.
posts.first: My trainer once told me to forget the bad round and remember the good entrance. I took that very seriously. I have a photo of the entrance on the fridge and nothing from the rest. Nobody in my house asks.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a glossy chestnut mare with a long wavy blonde mane and a gold earring, standing at the gate of a show ring and glancing sideways with a smirk. Text at the top reads: I looked incredible entering the show ring. Let's all remember that part.

posts.caption: The old farrier's truck had a dent in the tailgate from 1998. He drove it up this lane every six weeks, rain or frozen mud, and never once arrived early. When his knees finally gave out, his son took over the route and the same truck with a new bumper. The first visit, the boy asked me where his dad liked to park. I pointed at the exact spot by the water trough. He parked there and didn't say anything, and neither did I.
posts.first: I still keep his dad's old rasp on a nail in the tack room. The son doesn't know I kept it. I figure he'll find it when he's ready, and not before.
posts.alt: Painted storybook illustration of an elderly dappled gray horse with small round glasses standing in a sunlit hayloft, surrounded by an old hoof rasp, a faded photo, and a leather apron. posts.quote: My coworker asked if the horse is just a hobby. A hobby has never screamed at me from the barn at 5:30 for breakfast.
posts.first: She meant it kindly. I told her the horse gets fed before I do, then I went and looked up the hay delivery. She's never asked again. I think she's decided I'm just a person who leaves the house in a barn jacket.

posts.caption: Saturday started at six with a text from the barn manager that said, simply, 'rain.' I put my mug down like I'd won something. By seven the water was drumming on the tin roof and the hay smelled like September. I went out in my husband's coat to carry a warm bucket, and there she was, flat as a pancake in the straw with the barn cat on her back. I sat on an upturned bucket for an hour. Nobody called.
posts.first: There's one folding chair in the aisle that nobody else is allowed to use. It faces the stall. Some days I take my coffee out there and tell myself I'm checking on her. I am not checking on her.

posts.caption: The groomer had her clippers out of the case by 9:50. I could hear them from the tack room. I came around the corner and the pasture was empty, which is a neat trick for a horse the size of a delivery van. She was standing exactly where the fence disappears behind the hill, looking at a tree. I walked a quarter mile with a lead rope and a carrot. She accepted the carrot. She declined everything else.
posts.first: I once told a clipper salesman that my mare has opinions about noise. He asked what opinions. I said, you'll know them when she ends your career. He bought the quieter model.

posts.caption: The feed room latch is a two-step affair that I installed myself after the Great Pellet Incident two winters ago. I felt very clever. Then one Tuesday I found the door open, a scoop on the floor, and a round brown shape in the aisle looking at me like I was the one who'd left the lights on. I fixed the latch twice more. We're now on version four. I'm told version five is a padlock.
posts.first: I bought a padlock last week. It's still in the bag on the tack room shelf. Some part of me wants to keep believing in the latch. Some part of me wants to see what he'll do.
